title: is that a hat?
hookLine: what's under the turban, what the color means, and the plain steel circle on the wrist

lines: AND THE CIRCLE ON THE WRIST.
cards: Is that a hat? What's under there? Does the color mean something?
Sikhs who wear a turban hear these at school, at work and in the airport security line. The real answers are better than most people expect.
And there's a second thing that often needs explaining, on the wrist: a plain steel circle.

teach.h: KESH — HAIR, LEFT AS IT GREW.
teach.b: Start underneath. Many Sikhs keep their hair uncut all their lives, as a way of accepting the body as it was made. That's kesh.

teach.h: THE DASTAR — A CROWN YOU TIE.
teach.b: The turban, the dastar or pagg, covers and looks after that hair. So no, it isn't a hat that comes off with the weather.

Most who wear one tie it fresh each morning, over hair combed and knotted on top, yards of cloth wrapped layer by layer. It's a skill: first tries come out lopsided for everyone, and practice does the rest.
Sikh tradition remembers that in the Gurus' world a fine turban marked kings and nobles.
The tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, made it part of his community's identity, so every Sikh who ties one wears a crown, whatever family they come from.

teach.h: THE COLOR IS USUALLY A CHOICE.
teach.b: The color? For most, simply a choice, or what goes with the day. And not every Sikh wears one: some women do, many cover their hair with a scarf, and Sikhs keep the faith in different ways.
If you've cut your hair, you're every bit as welcome on this path. Now the wrist.
The kara is a plain steel bracelet: a circle with no beginning and no end, like the one God. Steel, not gold, on purpose. It isn't jewelry.
Sikhs often say that when your hand reaches for something, the kara gets there first and asks: should my hand be doing this?

how: Many Sikhs keep their hair uncut; men and some women tie a turban fresh each day, others cover their hair with a scarf, and many Sikhs, including some who don't keep the other articles of faith, wear a steel kara on the wrist. Everyone covers their head in the gurdwara.

p: a respectful word for the turban
a plain steel circle on the wrist

s: the color of a turban shows which group someone belongs to

the kara is steel, not gold, on purpose

games.q: you're the tenth Guru. in your world, fine turbans are worn by kings and nobles. what do you do?
o: ban turbans, so no one looks higher.
make the turban part of every Sikh's identity.

games.why: Guru Gobind Singh made it part of the community's identity. the effect was deliberate: every Sikh wears a crown.

the cloth, wrapped layer by layer
a crown, tied for the day

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, sit up and let the crown of your head rise, as if something precious rested there. On the second, touch your wrist, where a kara would sit.
On the third, think of one thing your hands will reach for today.

wordCard.voice: The turban. A crown tied fresh over hair left as it grew, and beside it, the steel kara. Third word.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: dastar, a respectful word for the turban; it comes from Persian.

carryVoice: Your line: a crown you tie yourself. Next time someone asks if it's a hat, that's the short answer. Day three.
